None of this separates P1 from P2 directly: both pause the first 5 nights. What matters for P1 vs P2 is nights 6 onward while equity is still under the trigger; on those the NVDA mean unit return was +0.288% (64 UP-trend nights, s.e. 0.53%) and the pooled mean was -0.004% (1,027 nights), i.e. no detectable edge either way.
sims.dollars_at_stake:
Very little, and at the moment nothing.
P1 and P2 are identical for the first 5 sessions of a pause and on every DOWN-trend night (both hold 0.25). They differ only from session 6 onward, while equity is still at or below the trigger, and only if the trend is UP: P1 holds 0.25 of equity, P2 holds 0.98. At $82 that gap is 0.73 x $82 = $59.86 of the 2x ETF.
Expected value of that gap per night, from NVDA history: $0.10 (all-night mean unit return +0.166%), $0.165 (UP-trend nights, +0.275%), $0.17 (the 64 actual UP-trend extension nights, +0.288%, s.e. 0.53%). Scaled to a 21-night month in which every night is such a night: about $2.1 to $3.6 in favour of P2. Using the pooled 11-name extension nights instead (mean -0.004%, n = 1,027) it is $0.00.
That month cannot occur: an extension lasts at most 14 nights, and NVDA averaged 2.67 UP-trend extension nights per pause episode (64 over 24 episodes). Realised in the simulation: P2 beat P1 by +0.169 log points in total over 26 years, which at $82 is about $0.58 per pause episode (reading B $0.63), or $0.044 a month averaged over all months (90% interval -$0.09 to +$0.20 a month).
Noise: one night moves the $59.86 gap by about $2.39 (1 s.d., unit-return s.d. 3.99%); over a full 14-night extension about $8.9. The expected difference is far inside that.
Right now: QQQ closed below its 200-session average on 2026-11-05 and 2026-11-06 (DOWN), so the pause size (1 share, about 0.25) equals the normal size (0.25) and P1 and P2 hold the same position: the difference is $0 unless the trend turns back UP while the pause is still in force after session 5. The 2026-11-09 bar is provisional and was not used.
sims.summary:
OUTCOME: keep the rule as written. Two of the three pre-registered criteria I can judge fail; criterion 4 (two implementations agree) is for the comparison with the other analyst.

(1) FAIL. NVDA, trend ON, p = 0.25: P2's g is higher than P1's in 2000-14 (+0.0842 vs +0.0778, diff +0.0064) but lower in 2015-26 (+0.2115 vs +0.2134, diff -0.0020; reading B -0.0014). It is also lower in 2015-26 at pause sizes 0.10 and 0.50.
(2) PASS. Worst drawdown is the same to two decimals: 47.33% vs 47.33% in the first half, 55.72% vs 55.72% in the second.
(3) FAIL. Whole-span P2-P1 is positive for 7 of 11 names and negative for 4 (reading B: 5 positive, 6 negative). 8 were needed.

How strong is this: it is a statistical tie, decided by the pre-registered rule and not by evidence that P1 is better. Whole-span P2-P1 for NVDA is +0.0026 %/night with a 90% interval of -0.0055 to +0.0117. The two variants differ on only 70 of 6,542 nights. The sign in each half comes from one episode: August 2003 (+0.226 log points for P2) and February-March 2020 (-0.214; the extension kept P1 at a quarter size through the crash). Without 2020 the second half would be +0.156 for P2; without 2003 the first half would be +0.002. With the trend rule off the half signs reverse (-0.0090 / +0.0057) and 4 of 11 names are positive, so the result also depends on the trend rule.

Other things the run shows:
- PAUSE itself cost growth for NVDA under the trend rule: P1-P0 = -0.0122 %/night whole span (interval -0.0227 to -0.0036), for a worst drawdown of 55.72% instead of 58.03%. Dropping it is not on the table.
- The event study agrees: after a P1 trigger under the trend rule, NVDA's next 5 nights averaged +4.1% log against +0.8% unconditionally (median +0.25%, so a few large rebounds carry it). Without the trend rule the sign reverses at 10 to 40 nights.
- The 10-night fixed pause (P2x10) beat P1 in both halves for NVDA (+0.0041 / +0.0038, whole-span interval +0.0007 to +0.0076), but it was a sensitivity, not the pre-registered candidate, and only 6 of 11 names agree. I would treat it as a hypothesis for a later cycle, not a result.
- Money: at $82 the choice is worth roughly $0.04 a month on average and $0 today, because the trend is DOWN and both variants hold the same quarter position.

Variants tried: 19 per name and trend setting (P0, plus P1, P2 in two re-arming readings, P3, P2x10 in two readings, each at three pause sizes), for 11 names and 2 trend settings = 418 simulations. The decision uses one cell only: P2 vs P1 at p = 0.25 with the trend rule on.

Checks: the hand-made 30-night series reproduces every pause start, end and equity value I worked out by hand for P0, P1, P2 (both readings), P3 and P2x10; a 24-night series confirms the size is min(b, p) on paused nights; on the real runs (66 name/trend/pause-size cells) the trigger condition recomputed with a numpy rolling maximum, the equity paths and all episode-structure rules match with zero violations.

The simulation follows the specification only: no earnings blackout, no whole-share rounding, underlying x2 instead of the real ETF.

- results.txt (main results plus the hand check; sections 1-11)
- results_main.txt, results_handtest.txt (the two parts separately)
- results.json (all numbers, machine-readable)
- loader.py, sim.py, run_l15.py, hand_test.py

sims.dollars_at_stake:
Very little, and possibly nothing right now.
- The two variants differ only on nights when P1 is still paused after the fifth night AND QQQ is at or above its mean. On such a night P2 holds 0.98 of equity and P1 holds 0.25: a gap of 0.73 x $82 = $59.86 of extra exposure.
- Expected value of that gap per night: $0.10 at NVDA's all-night mean (2r - 9bp = +0.166%); $0.17 at the mean seen on the 64 historical NVDA extension nights (+0.288%, standard error 0.53%, so not distinguishable from zero); $0.21 at the 2015-26 trend-UP mean (+0.359%); $0.00 at the pooled 11-name extension-night mean (-0.004%).
- Per month: a 21-session month has 5 nights common to both, so at most 16 extension nights (the longest seen for NVDA is 14): $1.6 to $3.4 in favour of P2 if the pause ran the whole month. A typical episode has far fewer: 2.7 biting extension nights on average (median 0), which is $0.26 to $0.57 per episode.
- Noise: the one-night standard deviation of the gap P&L is $1.89, about $7.6 over 16 nights, several times the expected difference.
- Long-run simulated average at $82: P2-P1 = +$0.05 per month over the whole span (+$0.11 in 2000-14, -$0.02 in 2015-26); with the trend rule off, -$0.10 per month.
- If QQQ is below its mean the gap is $0, because both variants then hold 0.25. In this data QQQ closed below the mean of its previous 199 closes on 2026-11-05 (647.05 vs 680.88) and 2026-11-06 (656.10 vs 681.01); the 11-09 bar is provisional and was not used, so I cannot state the trend state for tonight.

sims.summary:
OUTCOME: KEEP THE RULE AS WRITTEN (P1). Two of the three pre-registered criteria fail.

(1) FAIL. NVDA, trend rule on, pause size 0.25: P2 beats P1 in 2000-14 (g 0.0842 vs 0.0778 percent per night, +0.0064) but is lower in 2015-26 (0.2120 vs 0.2134, -0.0014). The second-half shortfall is tiny and well inside its interval [-0.0168,+0.0116], but the criterion asks for 'not lower in both halves' and it is lower in one.
(2) PASS. Worst drawdown is the same for P1 and P2 in both halves (47.33% and 55.72%).
(3) FAIL. Whole-span P2-P1 is positive for 5 names and negative for 6; the largest same-sign group is 6, short of 8.
Criterion (4), agreement with the other implementation, is not mine to judge.

The outcome does not depend on my readings: under the other P2 re-arm reading criterion 1 still fails (second half -0.0020) and the name count is 7 of 11; exit-date labelling, a common start date and a fresh second-half run all give the same verdict; so do pause sizes 0.10 and 0.50 and the trend-off table (where P2 is lower than P1 in both halves and 4 of 11 names are positive).

What the numbers say beyond the verdict: over the whole span P2-P1 for NVDA is +0.0028 percent per night [-0.0054,+0.0119], i.e. no detectable difference. It is the net of a handful of episodes (2003-08 and 2025-01 for P2, 2020-02 and 2019-05 for P1). Returns on the extension nights themselves look like ordinary nights (+0.288% vs +0.275% per unit of size for NVDA; -0.004% vs +0.074% pooled). The extension to 'until equity is back above the trigger' neither clearly helps nor clearly hurts; it lasts at most 19 nights with the trend rule on, and 13 of 24 NVDA episodes end at exactly 5 nights anyway.

Context only, since dropping PAUSE is not on the table: with the trend rule on, both P1 and P2 cost growth against P0 for NVDA (whole span -0.0122 and -0.0094 percent per night, both intervals below zero) and trim the worst drawdown by about 2 points (55.7% vs 58.0%).

Money: at $82 the expected difference is roughly $0.10 to $0.21 per extension night, $0.3 to $0.6 per typical episode and at most about $1.6 to $3.4 in a month in which the pause never lifts, against noise of about $7.6; it is $0 whenever QQQ is below its mean, as it was on the last two completed sessions in the data.

Two things to check: (a) c3_names_same_sign_count = 6 is the negative group; the positive count is 5. (b) The sensitivity P2x10 (a fixed 10 nights) beat P1 for NVDA in both halves (+0.0041 and +0.0038) but also fails criterion 3 at 5 of 11, and it was not the pre-registered candidate.

weaknesses: Few episodes. NVDA with the trend rule on has 24 P1 pause episodes in 26 years (10 in 2000-14, 14 in 2015-26). 13 last exactly 5 nights, so P1 and P2 hold the same sizes in them; only 9 contain an UP-trend extension night (64 such nights in all). The two variants' returns differ on 70 of 6,542 nights.

A handful of nights decide the sign. P2-P1 total log growth by year: 2003 +0.226, 2020 -0.214, 2025 +0.093, 2023 +0.089, 2019 -0.042, 2024 +0.038, 2015 -0.006, 2010 +0.002. The first-half result (+0.227) is the 14 nights of 2003-08-15 to 2003-09-04. The second-half result (-0.042) becomes +0.172 without 2020 and +0.122 without the single night of 2020-03-06 (NVDA -9.83% overnight, -0.164 on its own). So criterion 1 fails on one night; equally, P2's whole-span lead (+0.185) turns to -0.040 without 2003. Every interval for P2-P1 includes zero (second half -0.0168 to +0.0116, 48% of bootstrap draws positive). The data cannot tell P1 from P2; the outcome is a tie settled by the pre-registered rule.

Criterion 3 is close to a coin-flip count. It is 5 of 11 positive under one reading of P2 and 7 under the other, because INTC and QCOM flip on differences of about 0.002 percent per night. In 6 of 11 names (NVDA, AMD, INTC, MSFT, QCOM, AMAT) removing one calendar year flips the sign of the whole-span difference. For six of the ten other names the strategy loses money even with no pause (P0 g negative for INTC, MSFT, AMZN, QCOM, TXN, ORCL), so those are comparisons between losing paths.

Pause size. The NVDA pattern (P2 ahead in 2000-14, behind in 2015-26) holds at 0.10, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30 and 0.50, but the second-half shortfall ranges from -0.0014 to -0.0070 and the whole-span difference is about zero at 0.10 and 0.50 (+0.0005). The 11-name positive count is 6 / 5 / 5 at 0.10 / 0.25 / 0.50 (5 / 7 / 7 on the other reading). The live rule is exactly 1 share, not a fraction: at NVDL's 23.71 close on 2026-11-06 one share is 29% of $82, and that fraction moves with price and equity.

The result depends on the trend rule. With it off (82 episodes) P2 is behind P1 in both halves on the primary reading (-0.0068 / -0.0050, whole span -0.0060) and mixed on the other (-0.0090 / +0.0057); 4 of 11 names are positive; and the event study reverses (NVDA, 20 nights after a trigger: -0.0258 against +0.0162 unconditional, where the trend-on figures are +0.0621 against +0.0304). The trend rule is new this week and came from a backtest on these same bars. The simulation also applies it with QQQ's closing price, which is not known when the afternoon order is placed.

Knife-edge triggers (my probes, not pre-registered). A threshold of 0.81 instead of 0.80 turns the second half to +0.0065, which would pass criterion 1; 0.78, 0.79 and 0.82 leave it negative (-0.0064, -0.0062, -0.0049). A 15- or 25-session window gives a whole-span difference of +0.0001 or -0.0008. Changing the cost from 9bp to 0 or 20bp changes the number of P1 episodes from 24 to 20 or 29. The verdict on criterion 1 is not robust in either direction.

Criterion 2 does not look where the variants differ. The worst drawdown of each half falls in 2000-12 to 2002-07 and 2022-01 to 2023-02, when both variants hold the same size, so it is identical by construction. Inside 2020 P2's drawdown is 50.5% against P1's 37.2%, and inside 2019 32.2% against 27.0%; inside 2003 it is the other way round (P1 47.0%, P2 38.8%). 'Same worst drawdown' does not mean the same risk.

What the synthetic 2x leaves out. No 2x NVDA ETF existed for most of the sample: in these files NVDL has real bars only from 2022-12-13 and NVDX from 2023-10-19, so about 22 of 26 years are a model. On the 765 nights with real NVDX bars its close-to-open return averaged 0.054% a night below 2x NVDA (0.032% without two nights more than 3% apart), with night-to-night tracking error of 0.33% to 0.57%; the flat 9bp has to cover that plus two spreads. Also not modelled: fills near 15:52 and 09:31 instead of the official close and open; whole shares and the 1-share pause; the earnings-night cash rule (the 2003 episode starts after a -14.25% overnight gap on 2003-08-07 that may be an earnings reaction the live engine would have sat out; I did not verify the date); the KILL level; dividends for the ten other names.

Independence is limited. The two analysts' programs are built alike (same state variables, same bootstrap routine and seed), and my third version, written differently, matches both to 1e-16. That rules out coding slips, not a shared misreading of the rule; the one instruction that was ambiguous did produce different headline counts. The bootstrap resamples realised yearly differences without re-simulating paths, and with the difference concentrated in 8 calendar years its intervals are rough (the first-half lower bound is exactly zero because only 2003 and 2010 contribute).

Many variants, one decision. Each name was run with up to 7 variants at 3 pause sizes and 2 trend settings. The 10-night fixed pause beat P1 for NVDA in both halves (+0.0041 / +0.0038, whole-span interval +0.0007 to +0.0076), but it was a sensitivity, not the pre-registered candidate: a hypothesis for a later cycle, not a finding. The run also shows PAUSE itself cost growth with the trend rule on (P1-P0 -0.0122 percent per night, interval -0.0227 to -0.0036, for a worst drawdown of 55.7% instead of 58.0%); dropping it was excluded in advance and stays excluded.
adjudication.plain_summary:
Tested: when the account falls 20% below its recent high, PAUSE cuts the nightly position to about a quarter for five sessions, then keeps it small until the account recovers above the trigger. Would ending the pause after exactly five sessions be better? Replayed on 26 years of NVIDIA and ten other stocks.

Found: both analysts' programs, and my own, give identical results night for night. Their reports differed only because one instruction can be read two ways; the answer is the same under both. The five-session version grew slightly faster in 2000-2014 and slower in 2015-2026, with the same worst loss. It was ahead for 5 of 11 stocks (7 on the other reading); 8 were required.

Decision: keep the rule as written. This is a tie settled by the pre-agreed criteria, not proof the current rule is better; one night in March 2020 decides the second half.

Money: at $82, about 5 cents a month on average, at most about $2 expected over the longest possible pause, nothing in a pause's first five sessions.
